name: Belief Systems and the Power of the Bhakti Tradition

scenes.animation: A stormy sky over an old Indian town, with lightning labelled 'Political instability'. Beneath it, a small courtyard glows warmly where people of all backgrounds sing bhajans with a dholak and cymbals. Zippy, soaked from the rain, peeks in.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's storming out there, but these people are singing! How?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the story of this period, Zippy. From the 13th to the 17th centuries, politics was stormy, yet Indian culture kept growing richer.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds left to right: '4th century BCE: Megasthenes visits', 'Arab traders come for spices', then 'Early 13th century: new rulers' with a link card 'See Part 1: Reshaping India's Political Map'. Three pillars rise below: 'Traditions continue', 'Patronage by rulers of many backgrounds', 'People from all sections take part'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India always had visitors: traders, scholars and diplomats from Greece, Persia, Central Asia and beyond. It adopted and adapted the best of their cultures.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: From the early 13th century, new rulers brought different political ideas, art styles and beliefs. Through it all, three patterns stand out: traditions continued, rulers of many backgrounds supported the arts, and ordinary people took part.

scenes.animation: An old temple with a cracked wall appears in muted colours, then fades into a scene of a Hindu temple and a mosque standing in the same modern town. A question mark floats: 'How did diverse groups coexist?'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The beliefs of many invaders were very different from local traditions. Some plundered and destroyed ancient temples and sacred sites.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yet India's native belief systems continued, and Islam is also practised here along with other religions. How did society weather that time?

scenes.animation: A glowing path labelled 'Bhakti marga: path of devotion' leads to a light labelled 'Moksha'. Priests and ritual objects step aside while singers walk the path freely. A caption reads 'Crystallised by the 6th century'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One answer is bhakti, the path of devotion. It was one of many paths to moksha, and it needed no rituals or priests.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bhakti had taken shape by the 6th century. Now it grew popular again, with songs in local languages about love, compassion and equality.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up region by region with saint-poet portraits: Kabir and Ravidas in the north (present-day Uttar Pradesh), Guru Nanak journeying across regions, Mirabai in Rajasthan, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in the east, Tukaram, Dnyaneshwar and Namdev in the west, Purandaradasa and Kanakadasa in the south, Alvar and Nayanar hymns glowing in Tamil Nadu.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kabir, in the 15th century, sang of one god and questioned the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam. Ravidas, born in a family of leather-workers, sang of equality and oneness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Guru Nanak spread the message of one God and the equality of all. His teachings are preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mirabai sang in Rajasthan, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in the east, Tukaram and Namdev in the west, and Purandaradasa in the south. Purandaradasa is called the father of Carnatic music.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What was Kabir's flour line?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When wheat becomes flour, grains lose their differences. When one realises the divine, the difference between Ram and Rahim dissolves.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: learn one saint from each region with their key message. Questions often ask for three.

scenes.animation: The storm clears over the courtyard as three recap points appear on a painted scroll.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: despite political turmoil, Indian culture continued and grew richer. Two: bhakti, the path of devotion, needed no rituals or priests and used local languages. Three: saints like Kabir, Ravidas, Guru Nanak, Mirabai and Purandaradasa spread equality and oneness.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Songs beat storms. Got it!

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to spin like a whirling dervish, gets dizzy and crashes into a stack of tambourines. A Sufi musician walk-on laughs gently and helps him up.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: How do they spin so long without falling over?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Tremendous practice! For them, whirling is a kind of meditation. Let's meet the Sufis.

scenes.animation: A dargah courtyard at dusk: qawwals sing with harmonium and clapping. Name cards appear: 'Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti', 'Nizamuddin Auliya'. A word card reads 'Zikr: remembrance of God through chanting divine names'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sufism is a path of Islam focused on devotion and a personal search for god. Sufi saints sang devotional songs called qawwalis, mixing in local classical music.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Saints like Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya encouraged music as a way to connect with god.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sufis also used meditation, like zikr, and inner silence, much like Vedantic paths to moksha.

scenes.animation: Two rivers labelled 'Bhakti' and 'Sufi' flow side by side and merge into one stream labelled 'Unity and devotion'. Dara Shikoh sits between a pandit and a Muslim scholar, translating a manuscript titled 'Upanishads' into Persian.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dara Shikoh saw Vedanta and Sufism as meeting at one universal truth. He helped translate Upanishads into Persian.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the bhakti and Sufi traditions often overlapped, and poets wove ideas of unity into Indian literature.

scenes.animation: A music map: the north labelled 'Hindustani', the south labelled 'Carnatic'. Portraits pop up: Amir Khusro with a stamp and a caption 'qawwali'; Raja Mansingh Tomar in Gwalior with 'dhrupad, late 15th century'; Tansen walking into Akbar's court and taking a seat among the 'nine ratnas'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Classical music grew in two streams: Hindustani in the north and Carnatic in the south.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Amir Khusro, an Indo-Persian Sufi poet, is credited with developing the qawwali. It fused Indian, Persian and Arabic singing.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the late 15th century, Raja Mansingh Tomar of Gwalior raised dhrupad to new heights. Tansen became one of the nine ratnas of Akbar's court.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Did Tansen switch styles?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He was influenced by a Sufi saint, yet kept composing in praise of Krishna and Shiva. Indian culture accepted influences while keeping its core.

scenes.animation: A workshop bench: an old pakhawaj slowly morphs into a pair of tablas, and a sitar takes shape string by string. Rajasthani puppets and an unrolled pattachitra of the Ramayana dance at the side. An 'Exam Tip' card reads 'Carnatic: largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influences'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carnatic music developed largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influences.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Modern forms of the sitar and tabla evolved in these centuries. The tabla draws on the ancient pakhawaj. Storytelling also thrived, like puppetry in Rajasthan and pattachitra cloth paintings.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: don't mix up the streams. Hindustani is northern, Carnatic is southern.

scenes.animation: The tambourines line up to spell out three recap points as Neo reads them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Sufism is a devotional path of Islam, and saints like Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya used qawwali music. Two: bhakti and Sufi ideas overlapped, and Dara Shikoh saw them meeting. Three: music grew in Hindustani and Carnatic streams, with dhrupad, Tansen, sitar and tabla.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'll stick to tabla. Less dizzy.

name: Miniature Paintings, Gardens and Women in Society

scenes.animation: Zippy squints at a tiny painting through a huge magnifying glass and discovers an entire royal court, elephants and peacocks inside it. A little painted elephant waves back.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: This painting is smaller than my notebook, but there's a whole palace inside!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Welcome to miniature painting. Artists moved from painting walls to painting paper.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds: 'Cave art', 'Ajanta murals', 'Paper reaches India, 10th or 11th century', 'Rajput painting, 15th to late 19th century'. A Rajput painting fills with lotuses, banyan trees, cows, peacocks and Krishna defeating a whirlwind demon.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After paper reached India in the 10th or 11th century, artists shifted from walls to paper.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rajput paintings showed Hindu themes and symbols of beauty: lotuses, banyan trees, elephants, cows and peacocks. Abul Fazl wrote that few in the world could equal these painters.

scenes.animation: Inside Akbar's atelier, three artists pass one page along: one draws lines, one fills colours, one adds finishing touches. The finished page reads 'Razmnama: Persian Mahabharata'. Some painters then walk off towards a signpost 'Bikaner'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mughal miniatures, shaped by Persian influence, showed court scenes, landscapes and portraits. In Akbar's atelier, one artist drew lines, another filled colours, and a third finished.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Styles mixed. Some Mughal painters moved to Bikaner, and gardens and hunts entered Rajput paintings, while Hindu themes kept flourishing.

scenes.animation: A garden plan draws itself from above: a square split into four parts by water channels labelled 'Charbagh', with fountains and terraces added. It becomes Nishat Bagh in Srinagar, then the garden at Amer Fort.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Gardens are ancient in India. Words like udyana and vatika appear in the Rigveda and the epics.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Mughals brought the Persian charbagh: four parts with water channels, fountains and terraces. Nishat Bagh in Srinagar is an example.

scenes.animation: Split map of India. North: a woman in a ghunghat, then Razia Sultan unveiled on her throne leading troops, then Nur Jahan with a coin bearing her name. South: Hampi wall carvings of women wrestling, keeping accounts and playing music, with a queen's donation inscription.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Were women's lives the same everywhere?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. After the invasions, in parts of north India, purdah spread and women appeared less in public.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Still, Razia Sultan was the first and only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. Nur Jahan had coins minted in her name.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the south, life for women changed little. At Vijayanagara, women wrestled, kept accounts and made music, and queens donated villages to temples.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: say that the veil was largely confined to north India. That regional difference earns marks.

scenes.animation: The magnifying glass zooms out to show three recap points framed like miniature paintings.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Rajput and Mughal miniatures influenced each other in style and colour. Two: Mughal gardens used the Persian charbagh design. Three: women's status varied by region, from purdah in the north to active public life in the south.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: That tiny elephant is still waving at me.

scenes.animation: Zippy lands in a 17th-century temple mandapa where children sit in rows writing on sand with sticks. He looks around for benches and a blackboard, confused.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Where are the desks? Is this even a school?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is! Back then, a temple mandapa or a priest's house could be a classroom.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up learning centres: gurukulas, mathas and temple schools; Kanchipuram and Sringeri glowing in the south; madrasas with 'Arabic, Persian, Hindavi'. A dark patch marks 'Nalanda and Vikramashila destroyed, late 12th century'. A scroll reads 'Pietro Della Valle, 1623: children learn reading, writing, arithmetic'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila in the late 12th century was an immense loss. Yet learning continued in gurukulas, mathas, temple schools, viharas and pathshalas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kanchipuram and Sringeri were famous for advanced learning. Madrasas taught Arabic, Persian and Hindavi.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1623, the Italian traveller Pietro Della Valle saw children in coastal Karnataka learning reading, writing and arithmetic.

scenes.animation: A handloom clacks in Banaras. Weavers from Gujarat arrive carrying looms; gold zari threads shimmer into a brocade sari with flowers and birds. A 'GI Tag' seal stamps it. Then a pashmina shawl unrolls with a teardrop-shaped buta motif.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Crafts were taught by apprenticeship, in families or guilds. With Akbar's encouragement, weavers from Gujarat moved to Banaras.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Zari and brocades became part of the Banarasi sari's style, which now has a GI tag. Pashmina shawls from Ladakh and Kashmir wool carried Persian-style buta motifs.

scenes.animation: Books fly between two shelves labelled 'Sanskrit' and 'Persian': Lilavati translated by Faizi, Rajatarangini, and Dara Shikoh's 52 Upanishads, which then sail off towards Europe. Language labels light up: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Odia, Bengali, Marathi, Hindavi.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Literature flourished in many languages. Kavindra Paramesvara translated the Mahabharata into Bengali.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Persian became the court language. Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati and Kalhana's Rajatarangini were translated into Persian.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dara Shikoh translated 52 Upanishads into Persian. They later reached Europe and influenced thinkers there.

scenes.animation: A train travels from Lucknow to Hyderabad; speech bubbles change from 'Urdu' to 'Dakhini' as the train crosses the Deccan. Amir Khusro appears with a badge 'Father of Urdu literature'. A book stamped 'Eighth Schedule' closes.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Where did Urdu come from?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Urdu grew in the Ganga-Yamuna plains from Hindavi, taking words from Arabic and Persian. South of the Deccan, it became Dakhini.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Amir Khusro is called the father of Urdu literature. Urdu is listed in the Eighth Schedule of our Constitution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember that Dara Shikoh translated 52 Upanishads. The number is a favourite one-mark question.

scenes.animation: The sand-writing children spell out three recap points in the mandapa.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: despite losing Nalanda and Vikramashila, learning continued in local institutions. Two: crafts like Banarasi weaving grew through apprenticeships and new techniques. Three: translations between Sanskrit and Persian flourished, and Urdu developed from Hindavi.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm writing my homework in sand from now on.

name: Science, Architecture and Cultural Exchange in Daily Life

scenes.animation: At a school canteen, Zippy holds a samosa in one hand and a jalebi in the other. A thought bubble shows a Persian chef shrugging.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Samosa and jalebi are one hundred per cent Indian, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They are Indian now, but they have a travel story! First, let's look at science.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds step by step: '14th century: Narayana Pandita writes Ganitakaumudi', 'Madhava: infinite series and pi, Kerala School', '1500: Nilakantha Somayaji's planetary model', '1543: Copernicus'. A diagram shows Mercury and Venus circling the Sun.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: India's culture of enquiry continued. Pure zinc was made by a special distillation process, used for the first time in the world.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the south, Madhava made pioneering contributions to calculus, including an exact value of pi as an infinite series. He founded the Kerala School.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1500, Nilakantha Somayaji described Mercury and Venus going round the Sun, decades before Copernicus in 1543.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Saltpetre was used to cool water, and Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicine were widely practised.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up monuments one by one: the stone wheels of Konark's Surya Mandir (13th century), the Jain temple at Ranakpur (15th century), the Sheesh Mahal at Amer sparkling under one lamp, Hampi's temples, and the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam being rebuilt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Architecture reached great heights: the Surya Mandir at Konark, the Jain temple at Ranakpur, and the mirrored Sheesh Mahal at Amer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Under Krishnadevaraya, Hampi saw a golden age of temple building. Temples that were destroyed were rebuilt, like the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam.

scenes.animation: A kitchen split screen: a Persian 'sambuseh' stuffed with meat and nuts morphs into a samosa filled with potatoes and peas; a floral 'zalabiyeh' with honey and rose water morphs into round jalebi coils in sugar syrup. A clay oven pops out a naan.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The samosa comes from the Persian sambuseh, stuffed with meat and nuts. Indian cooks switched to potatoes and peas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Jalebi comes from zalabiyeh, which used honey and rose water. Naan from the clay oven is a Persian influence too.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The influence went both ways. Akbar is said to have cut down on meat, partly under Jain and Hindu influence.

scenes.animation: A fashion parade: a noble in a jama and pyjama, a woman in a fine muslin dupatta, and a model in an angrakha, followed by women in regional saris. Zippy tries on a turban that covers his eyes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In clothing, the jama and pyjama were adopted at court. The angrakha is believed to have come from Persian court fashion, adapted to Indian fabrics.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And the sari, in all its regional styles, continued.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in 'cultural exchange' answers, give one example each from food and clothing.

scenes.animation: Neo stands beside a canteen menu board where three recap points are chalked in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: science advanced, from zinc distillation to Madhava's work on calculus and Nilakantha's planetary model. Two: temples and palaces were built, and destroyed temples were rebuilt. Three: cultures mixed in daily life, giving us samosa, jalebi, naan and the angrakha.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: History tastes delicious!
